claims.text: The initial Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy is single-phase BCC.
Asymmetric XRD peaks in the initial alloy indicate dendritic versus interdendritic compositional micro-segregation.
The initial alloy has low room-temperature fracture strain.
Adding approximately 4 at.% Cr induces a complex C14 or C15 multicomponent Laves phase.
The Cr-induced Laves phase occupies approximately 4 vol.%.
The Laves phase forms a reticulated or interconnected network at interdendritic boundaries.
A reticulated Laves-phase network impedes crack extension by deflecting or pinning cracks and increasing crack-path tortuosity.
Cr solute produces lattice distortion in the BCC matrix.
The size mismatch between Cr and Hf, Zr, and Ti creates local strain fields that impede dislocation motion and cause solid-solution hardening.
Micro-segregation generates local Cr-rich zones that preferentially nucleate the Laves phase in interdendritic regions.
Cooling conditions that retain segregation gradients while allowing secondary-phase nucleation can preserve the proposed two-phase microstructure.
Cr addition contracts the BCC lattice parameter because Cr is smaller than Hf, Zr, and Ti.
Cr addition produces a significant increase in hardness.
The interconnected Laves-phase network is embrittling and therefore keeps fracture strain below theoretical expectations despite hardening.
The Cr-free Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr baseline contains no Laves phase.
A BCC lattice-parameter contraction greater than 0.01 Å indicates enough dissolved Cr to destabilize the single-phase BCC state in favor of Laves-phase formation.
If the BCC lattice contraction does not exceed the proposed threshold, the Laves phase will not form or will remain isolated.
Heat treatment and slow cooling can generate a secondary phase and coincide with increased hardness and severe brittleness in a related refractory alloy.

contradictions.description: The Laves network is described as a crack-deflection and crack-pinning barrier that impedes crack extension, but it is also assigned an embrittling role that maintains low fracture strain. The hypothesis does not explain when crack deflection is beneficial versus when interconnected phase-boundary propagation dominates.

Cracks are said both to be pinned by the Laves phase and to propagate along its boundaries. These are distinct crack-interaction regimes and are presented together without a criterion governing which occurs.
